label: L20
title: Missing Data Imputations
brief: Missing data appear in almost every application, and the task is to turn a partially observed matrix $X \in \mathbb{R}^{n\times p}$ into a complete $X^{imp}$ by choosing values $w_{id}$ for the missing cells $(i,d) \in M$. Missingness can be completely at random (MCAR), at random given the observed data (MAR) or not at random (NMAR); simple fixes drop rows or columns or impute means, while classic methods (EM, PMM/MICE, KNN impute) rely on distributional assumptions or heuristics and degrade as the missing share grows. The optimization view treats imputation as a joint problem over imputed values and model variables: opt.knn minimizes the summed squared distances from each incomplete row to its $K$ nearest neighbors, a non-convex mixed-integer problem solved with block coordinate descent or coordinate descent from random warm starts. The same template gives opt.svm and opt.tree and handles categorical features; the cost is non-increasing and the algorithm terminates in finitely many iterations, though only at a local optimum. On 84 UCI data sets with 10-50% missing under MCAR and NMAR, the cross-validated opt.impute has the lowest MAE most often and its advantage, including on downstream classification and regression, grows with the missing percentage.
kp: Problem: given $X$ with missing set $M = \{(i,d): x_{id} \text{ missing}\}$, produce a complete $X^{imp}$ with imputed values $w_{id}$, $(i,d) \in M$.
Mechanisms: MCAR $f(M|X)=f(M)$; MAR $f(M|X)=f(M|X_{obs})$; NMAR is everything else (e.g. survival analysis, customer surveys).
Simple solutions: complete-case analysis (drop rows), complete-feature analysis (drop columns), mean imputation.

Classic methods and issues: EM (strong distributional assumptions, breaks with singular covariance), PMM/MICE multiple imputation (slow, does not scale, not very accurate), KNN impute (heuristic, poor at high missingness).
opt.knn: $\min \sum_{i\in I}\sum_{j\ne i} z_{ij}\|w_i - w_j\|_2^2$ s.t. known entries fixed, $\sum_{j\ne i} z_{ij} = K$, $z_{ij} \in \{0,1\}$, where $I$ is the set of rows with a missing coordinate.
The problem is non-convex, nonlinear and integer, so global methods do not scale; fast first-order methods (BCD, CD) with random warm starts solve $n \sim 100{,}000$s, $p \sim 1{,}000$s in minutes.

BCD alternates a sorting step for $Z$ and a closed-form linear solve $w_d = Q^{-1}R x_d$ per dimension; CD sets each $w_{id}$ to a weighted average of its neighbors and of points that have it as a neighbor.
General framework: $\min c(U,W,V;X)$ with model auxiliary variables $U$, continuous imputations $W$ and categorical imputations $V$; instances are opt.knn, opt.svm and opt.tree.

Algorithm 1 alternates updating $U$ and $(W,V)$; the cost is non-increasing and it stops within $\lceil c_{init}/\delta_0 \rceil$ iterations, but only at a local optimum, so use about 5 random restarts.
Results on 84 UCI data sets: opt.cv wins on MAE most often, and its gains over benchmark.cv and of opt.mi over mice in downstream accuracy and $R^2$ grow with the missing percentage.

topics.x: Missing values are common in health records, genomics, time series and surveys; imputation serves the completed data set itself (the Netflix problem), statistical inference, or a downstream ML model. The mechanism matters: MCAR, MAR or NMAR, and naive fixes like dropping rows or columns or mean imputation are the baselines.

EM maximizes the observed-data likelihood by alternating expectation and maximization steps but needs strong distributional assumptions. Multiple imputation with PMM (the MICE package) captures imputation variance for inference but is slow, while KNN impute averages the nearest rows that have the value, which breaks down when many rows are incomplete.

Imputed values and neighbor assignments are optimized jointly: minimize the summed squared distances from every incomplete row to its $K$ chosen neighbors, with known entries fixed. Binary $z_{ij}$ make it a non-convex mixed-integer problem, attacked with first-order methods.

With $W$ fixed, the best $Z$ picks each row's $K$ nearest neighbors (a sort). With $Z$ fixed, $W$ solves a convex quadratic: BCD solves a linear system $Q w_d = R x_d$ per dimension, CD updates one entry at a time by a weighted average of neighbors.

Any imputation model with auxiliary variables $U$ and cost $c(U,W,V;X)$ fits: opt.knn (neighbor indicators), opt.svm (SVM regression and classification per feature) and opt.tree (same-leaf indicators). Algorithm 1 alternates model fitting and imputation, with a monotone cost, finite termination and random restarts for the non-convexity.

Experiments on 84 UCI data sets with 10-50% missing under MCAR and NMAR compare mean, knn, iknn, pmm, bpca and the opt methods by MAE and by downstream accuracy and $R^2$. Cross-validated opt.impute wins most often and its advantage grows with missingness, with significant downstream gains at higher missing percentages.

cards.f: Formal statement of the missing data problem.
cards.b: Given $X \in \mathbb{R}^{n\times p}$ with missing entries, produce a complete $X^{imp}$ with imputed values $w_{id}$ for $(i,d) \in M = \{(i,d): x_{id} \text{ is missing}\}$; $n$ = observations, $p$ = features.
cards.x: Known entries stay fixed; only cells in $M$ are decision variables.

cards.b: MCAR: $f(M|X) = f(M)$, missingness independent of the data. MAR: $f(M|X) = f(M|X_{obs})$, depends only on observed values. NMAR: all other cases (e.g. survival analysis, customer surveys).
cards.x: NMAR means the missingness depends on the unobserved values themselves.

cards.b: (1) The completed data set itself (e.g. the Netflix problem). (2) Statistical inference. (3) Input to a downstream machine learning model.
cards.x: Which use you care about decides the metric: cell accuracy vs downstream performance.

cards.f: Three simple solutions to missing data.
cards.b: Complete-case analysis: drop rows with missing values. Complete-feature analysis: drop columns with missing values. Mean imputation: replace each missing value by the row/column mean.
cards.x: With many partly missing columns, complete-case analysis can discard most of the data.

cards.f: How does EM imputation work and what are its issues?
cards.b: Maximize the likelihood $L(X_{obs}|\theta)$ by iterating an E-step $q(\theta|\theta^*) = E[L(\theta|X_{obs},X_{miss})|X_{obs},\theta^*]$ and an M-step $\theta^* = \arg\max_\theta q(\theta|\theta^*)$ until convergence (e.g. Gaussian mixtures). Issues: strong distributional assumptions; breaks with singular covariance matrices.
cards.x: A heuristic around a parametric model, not a direct imputation objective.

cards.f: What is multiple imputation with Predictive-Mean Matching (PMM)?
cards.b: Multiple imputation pools many imputed data sets to capture the variance of imputed values, which helps statistical inference. PMM fits a linear model predicting one column and samples from the posterior; MICE generalizes it to many columns. Issues: slow, does not scale to high dimensions, not very accurate.
cards.x: Multiple imputation targets valid inference, not just point accuracy.

cards.b: Impute $x_{id}$ from the $K$ points closest to $x_i$, using only points with a known value in dimension $d$ as neighbors and skipping missing dimensions when computing distances. Weaknesses: highly heuristic; performs poorly with large missing percentages because many points cannot serve as neighbors.
cards.x: Sequential/iterative KNN are heuristic fixes on a heuristic, with little gain.

cards.f: Why is opt.knn solved with first-order methods rather than to global optimality?
cards.b: It is a non-convex, nonlinear integer optimization problem and global methods do not scale; BCD or CD with random warm starts find high-quality solutions for $n \sim 100{,}000$s, $p \sim 1{,}000$s in minutes.
cards.x: Trade a global guarantee for scale.

cards.f: BCD for opt.knn: the $Z$-update with $W$ fixed.
cards.b: $\partial c/\partial z_{ij} = \|w_i - w_j\|_2^2$ and $\sum_{j\ne i} z_{ij} = K$, so set $z_{ij}=1$ for the $K$ nearest neighbors of $w_i$ and 0 otherwise: a sort.
cards.x: Linear objective in $Z$ with a cardinality constraint: pick the $K$ smallest costs.

cards.f: BCD for opt.knn: the $W$-update with $Z$ fixed.
cards.b: Setting $\partial c/\partial w_{id} = 0$ for every missing entry gives, per dimension $d$, a linear system $Q w_d = R x_d$ in the missing values $w_d$ and known values $x_d$; with $Q \succeq 0$ (WLOG) the closed form is $w_d = Q^{-1}R x_d$.
cards.x: With $Z$ fixed the objective is a convex quadratic in $W$.

cards.f: Coordinate descent update for one missing entry $w_{id}$.
cards.b: $w_{id} = \dfrac{\sum_{j=1}^n z_{ij}x_{jd} + \sum_{j\in I} z_{ji}x_{jd}}{K + \sum_{j\in I} z_{ji}}$, with $x_{jd} := w_{jd}$ when that entry is itself imputed.
cards.x: A weighted average of $i$'s $K$ neighbors and of every point that has $i$ as a neighbor.

cards.f: Ingredients of the general opt.impute formulation.
cards.b: Imputed continuous $w_{id}$, $(i,d)\in M_0$; imputed categorical $v_{id}$, $(i,d)\in M_1$; known continuous/categorical values fixed on $N_0$, $N_1$; auxiliary model variables $U$; cost $c(U,W,V;X)$; constraints $(U,W,V) \in \mathcal{U}$.
cards.x: Swap the model (KNN, SVM, tree) by changing $U$, $c$ and $\mathcal{U}$.

cards.b: $t^d_{ij} = 1$ if $(w_j,v_j)$ falls in the same leaf as $(w_i,v_i)$ in the decision tree that predicts feature $d$, 0 otherwise; the cost sums $t^d_{ij}(w_{id}-w_{jd})^2$ and $t^d_{ij}\mathbb{1}\{v_{id}\ne v_{jd}\}$.
cards.x: Like opt.knn, but 'neighbors' are leaf-mates of a tree built per feature.

cards.b: $c(U,W,V;X)$ is non-increasing under BCD and CD updates; the algorithm terminates within $\lceil c(U_{init},W_{init},V_{init};X)/\delta_0 \rceil$ iterations; $c$ is non-convex, so the global optimum is not guaranteed. In practice, 5 random restarts keeping the lowest objective work well.
cards.x: Monotone plus bounded below means finite stopping, not global optimality.

cards.f: How is imputation quality measured in the experiments?
cards.b: Mean Absolute Error over the missing cells, $\frac{1}{|M|}\sum_{(i,d)\in M} |w_{id} - x_{id}|$, plus downstream performance: out-of-sample accuracy for classification (Optimal Trees, SVM) and out-of-sample $R^2$ for regression (Lasso, SVR).
cards.x: The true $x_{id}$ are known because the missingness was generated on complete data sets.

quiz.q: Which condition defines data Missing Completely At Random (MCAR)?
o: $f(M|X) = f(M|X_{obs})$
$f(M|X)$ depends on the missing values
$f(X|M) = f(X)$ only for observed rows
quiz.e: MCAR: missingness does not depend on the data at all. $f(M|X) = f(M|X_{obs})$ is MAR.

quiz.q: In a customer survey, respondents with very high incomes tend to skip the income question. Which mechanism is this?
o: Not missing at random (NMAR)
Missing completely at random (MCAR)
Missing at random (MAR)
Complete-case missingness
quiz.e: Missingness depends on the unobserved income value itself, which is neither MCAR nor MAR (MAR depends only on observed values). Customer surveys are the lecture's NMAR example.

o: Drops every observation (row) that has a missing value
Drops every feature (column) that has a missing value
Imputes each missing value with the column mean
Imputes using the complete rows as neighbors
quiz.e: Complete-case removes rows; complete-feature removes columns.

quiz.q: A data set has 10 features, each missing independently with probability 0.1 (MCAR). Roughly what fraction of rows survives complete-case analysis?
o: About 35%
About 90%
About 10%
About 65%
quiz.e: A row survives only if all 10 entries are present: $0.9^{10} \approx 0.349$. 90% is the per-entry rate, not the per-row rate; 65% is the fraction of rows dropped.

quiz.q: Which issue does the lecture attribute to EM imputation?
o: Strong distributional assumptions; it breaks with singular covariance matrices
It cannot handle continuous features
It always drops incomplete rows
It requires labeled outcomes
quiz.e: EM needs a parametric model (e.g. Gaussian mixtures) and fails when the covariance is singular. It does not drop rows or need labels.

quiz.q: Why does KNN impute perform poorly when a large percentage of data is missing?
o: Only points with a known value in the target dimension can be neighbors, so many points cannot be used
Distances cannot be computed between any incomplete rows
It requires a Gaussian assumption that fails
It imputes all missing values with the global mean
quiz.e: Candidate neighbors must have dimension $d$ observed, and the pool shrinks as missingness grows. Distances are still computed by skipping missing dimensions, so the second option is wrong.

quiz.q: What is multiple imputation (e.g. PMM with MICE) mainly useful for?
o: Statistical inference, by capturing the variance of imputed values across many imputations
Speeding up imputation on high-dimensional data
Imputing categorical variables only
Guaranteeing the globally optimal imputation
quiz.e: Pooling many imputed results reflects imputation uncertainty for inference. The lecture calls PMM slow and unable to scale to high dimensions.

quiz.q: In opt.knn, what is the index set $I$?
o: Observations with at least one missing coordinate
All observations
Observations with no missing values
Features with at least one missing value
quiz.e: Only incomplete rows need neighbors in the objective; complete rows can still serve as neighbors.

quiz.q: With $n = 1{,}000$ observations of which 200 have a missing coordinate, how many binary variables $z_{ij}$ does opt.knn (as on p.16) have?
In block coordinate descent for opt.knn, how is $Z$ updated when $W$ is fixed?
o: Sort distances and set $z_{ij}=1$ for each row's $K$ nearest neighbors
Solve the linear system $Qw_d = Rx_d$
Take a gradient step on $z_{ij}$
Solve a mixed-integer program to optimality
quiz.e: With $W$ fixed the cost is linear in $Z$ with coefficient $\|w_i-w_j\|^2$ and $\sum_j z_{ij}=K$, so the $K$ smallest distances win. The linear system is the $W$-update.

quiz.q: Coordinate descent for opt.knn with $K=2$: point $i$'s two neighbors have values 3 and 5 in dimension $d$, and one other incomplete point $j$ has $i$ among its neighbors, with value 8 in dimension $d$. What is the updated $w_{id}$?
quiz.e: $w_{id} = (3 + 5 + 8)/(K + 1) = 16/3$. Using only $i$'s own neighbors gives 4, which misses the term for points that list $i$ as a neighbor.

quiz.q: How should the coordinate descent update for $w_{id}$ be interpreted?
o: A weighted average of $x_i$'s $K$ nearest neighbors and of all points that have $x_i$ as a neighbor
The mean of column $d$ over complete rows
The value predicted by a linear regression on the other features
The median of the $K$ nearest neighbors
quiz.e: Both directions of the neighbor relation appear in the objective, so both enter the average. Column mean is mean imputation.

quiz.q: Algorithm 1 starts with cost $c_{init} = 12.5$ and threshold $\delta_0 = 0.5$. What is the most iterations it can run?
o: Unbounded, since the problem is non-convex
quiz.e: Each iteration that continues lowers the cost by more than $\delta_0$ and the cost is non-negative, so at most $\lceil 12.5/0.5 \rceil = 25$. Non-convexity affects global optimality, not termination.

quiz.q: Which statement about Algorithm 1 (opt.impute) is FALSE?
o: It converges to the global optimum because each block update is optimal
The cost is non-increasing under BCD and CD updates
It terminates in a finite number of iterations
Several random restarts, keeping the lowest objective, work well in practice
quiz.e: Exact block updates make the cost monotone but the cost is non-convex, so only a local minimum is reached. That is why 5 random restarts are used.

o: Points $j$ and $i$ fall in the same leaf of the tree that predicts feature $d$
Point $j$ is among the $K$ nearest neighbors of $i$
Feature $d$ is missing for both $i$ and $j$
The tree for feature $d$ splits on point $j$
quiz.e: opt.tree replaces KNN's neighbor indicators with same-leaf indicators from a tree per feature. The KNN indicator is $z_{ij}$.

quiz.q: Which metric measures imputation accuracy in the experiments?
o: Mean absolute error over the missing cells
Out-of-sample $R^2$ of a Lasso model
Log-likelihood of the observed data
Fraction of rows imputed
quiz.e: MAE $= \frac{1}{|M|}\sum |w_{id}-x_{id}|$. $R^2$ and accuracy measure downstream tasks.

quiz.q: Three missing cells are imputed as 2.0, 5.5 and 1.0; their true values are 2.5, 5.0 and 2.0. What is the MAE?
For downstream classification at 10% missing, opt.mi - mice = -0.0001 (adjusted p = 1.0000), while at 50% it is +0.0052 (p < 0.001). What is the correct reading?
o: No significant difference at low missingness; opt.mi's advantage becomes significant as missingness grows
mice is significantly better at 10% missing
opt.mi is significantly better at every missing level
The differences are too small to be significant at any level
quiz.e: p = 1.0 means no evidence of a difference at 10%; at 50% the gain is significant. This matches the general pattern that opt.impute's edge grows with the missing percentage.

written.q: (a) Formulate opt.knn imputation as an optimization problem, defining all variables and sets. (b) Derive the coordinate descent update for a single missing entry $w_{id}$ with $Z$ fixed, and interpret it. (c) Explain how block coordinate descent differs and why the overall method only finds a local optimum.
written.m:
(a) Let $M$ be the missing cells and $I$ the rows with at least one missing coordinate. Decision variables: $w_{id}$ for $(i,d)\in M$ (known $w_{id}=x_{id}$ otherwise) and $z_{ij}\in\{0,1\}$, equal to 1 if $w_j$ is among the $K$ nearest neighbors of $w_i$. Problem: $\min \sum_{i\in I}\sum_{j
e i} z_{ij}\|w_i-w_j\|_2^2$ s.t. $w_{id}=x_{id}$ for $(i,d)
otin M$, $\sum_{j
e i} z_{ij}=K$ for $i\in I$, $Z\in\{0,1\}^{|I|	imes(n-1)}$. (b) The terms containing $w_{id}$ are $\sum_j z_{ij}(w_{id}-x_{jd})^2$ (i's own neighbors) and $\sum_{j\in I} z_{ji}(x_{jd}-w_{id})^2$ (points that have $i$ as neighbor), with $x_{jd}:=w_{jd}$ for imputed entries. Setting the derivative to zero: $w_{id}(K+\sum_{j\in I} z_{ji}) = \sum_j z_{ij}x_{jd} + \sum_{j\in I} z_{ji}x_{jd}$, so $w_{id}$ is the weighted average of $i$'s $K$ neighbors and of all points listing $i$ as a neighbor. (c) BCD updates $Z$ by sorting (each row takes its $K$ nearest) and then all missing values of a dimension at once by solving $Q w_d = R x_d$ in closed form; CD updates entries one by one. Each step cannot increase the cost, so the algorithm stops in finitely many iterations, but the joint problem is non-convex and integer, so the result depends on the warm start; random restarts (about 5) and keeping the lowest objective help.
k: Correct sets M and I and variables w, z
Correct objective and constraints, including sum z = K and fixed known entries
Correct closed-form CD update and its interpretation
BCD: sorting for Z, linear system Q w_d = R x_d for W
Monotone cost, finite termination, non-convex so local optimum and restarts

written.q: A hospital data set has 40% of lab values missing, and labs are ordered more often for sicker patients. (a) Which missingness mechanism is most plausible, and why does it matter? (b) Compare complete-case analysis, mean imputation, KNN impute and opt.impute for this setting using the lecture's arguments and results. (c) How would you choose among opt.knn, opt.svm and opt.tree, and how would you judge success if the goal is a mortality model?
written.m: (a) Missingness depends on patient condition; if that is captured by observed variables it is MAR ($f(M|X)=f(M|X_{obs})$), and if it depends on the unobserved lab values themselves it is NMAR. The mechanism matters because methods built for MCAR can bias results; the lecture evaluates under both MCAR and NMAR. (b) Complete-case analysis would drop most rows when many labs are partly missing and keep a non-representative subset. Mean imputation is simple but ignores relations between features. KNN impute is heuristic and degrades at high missingness because only rows with the value observed can be neighbors. opt.impute treats imputation as an optimization problem without strong distributional assumptions, scales to large data, and in the experiments its cross-validated version wins on MAE most often, with the gap over benchmarks growing with the missing percentage (e.g. downstream $R^2$ gain of opt.cv over benchmark.cv rises from 0.0034 at 10% to 0.0237 at 50%). (c) Use opt.cv: cross-validate among opt.knn, opt.svm and opt.tree and pick the best, using all three within the general framework (opt.tree and opt.knn handle categorical variables directly). Judge success by the downstream task, out-of-sample performance of the mortality model, and if possible MAE on artificially masked known values; use opt.mi if valid inference with imputation uncertainty is needed.

Complete-case loses many rows and biases sample
Mean and KNN impute weaknesses, KNN fails at high missingness
opt.impute advantages: no strong distributional assumptions, scalable, accuracy grows with missingness
Success measured downstream and/or by MAE on masked values
